title: Bootstrap: how sure is the tree?
summary: Predict which grouping the data supports least, then resample and see.

prompts.concept: These eight sequences share a true tree, but the alignment is deliberately short. Build the NJ tree, then step to the end to ask: how sure are we that each grouping is real?
prompts.math: A short internal branch leaves few sites where its grouping differs from the rest — exactly the sites a resample can miss.

prompts.concept: Before you run, make a prediction: which internal branch of the inferred tree will the data support least? Click that branch — terminal branches don't count — then run the bootstrap.
prompts.math: Each replicate resamples the 300 columns with replacement and rebuilds the tree; a grouping's support is the share of successful replicate trees that contain it.
prompts.reveal: The weakest grouping sits on the shortest internal branch of the true tree — at 300 columns it has recorded very few informative sites, so many resamples rebuild a different split there.

prompts.concept: Support is an estimate, too. Re-run with a different bootstrap Seed and watch the labels move by a few points — about ±5 near 50% at 100 replicates. Then raise Replicates to 1,000 and run again: the numbers steady to roughly ±1.6.
prompts.math: Resampling error shrinks like 1/√B: near 50% support it is about ±5 points at 100 replicates and ±1.6 at 1,000.

prompts.concept: Now try more data. Raise Length to 3,000 — ten times as many columns — and run again. Watch what happens to that grouping's support.
prompts.math: Signal scales with sites: the same tree under 10× the columns puts ~10× the expected substitutions on every branch, short ones included.

prompts.concept: Read the numbers carefully: when a grouping shows 87, it means 87 of 100 resampled datasets rebuilt that grouping — not that the grouping has an 87% chance of being true. The bootstrap measures consistency under resampling, not the probability of being right — so don't overinterpret differences of a few points either.
